That this government take steps to negotiate the lowering of tariffs placed on Canadian fish exports by the European Economic Community so that Canadians are competitive with the preferential rates given by the European Economic Community to Norway and Iceland.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION THAT ONTARIO PREMIER RECOGNIZE LINGUISTIC DUALITY OF CANADA-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
Whereas a nation, in drafting its constitution, should do so with respect and in a spirit of generosity towards its minorities; and whereas it is vital to recognize more fully and to protect Canada's duality, I move, seconded by the member for Missis-quoi (Mr. Bachand):
That this House invite forthwith the Premier of Ontario, William Davis, to introduce in the Ontario Legislature now in session, a resolution to the effect that Ontario recognizes the linguistic duality of Canada and requests that it be bound by sections 14(2), 18(2), 19(2) and 20(2), which would make it possible for all French-speaking Canadians-wherever they may reside in Canada- when coming to Ontario, to have access to that province's parliamentary and judicial institutions and government services in the same manner as all Englishspeaking Canadians have had access to the same institutions in Quebec for over 114 years.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
Hundreds of thousands of Ontarians have French as their mother tongue, and it is only fair to ask that their cultural heritage and language rights should be protected. Considering the fact that the government of Ontario persists in refusing to recognize the right of Franco-Ontarians to communicate with their government and legislature and with their Ontario courts in the official language of their choice, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Heap):
That the House of Commons amend the constitutional resolution to make Section 133 of the British North America Act, in other words, Sections 16 to 20 and 22 of the constitutional resolution, applicable to Ontario, and to provide for entrenchment of the language rights of Franco-Ontarians in the Charter of Rights and our Constitution.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I did meet at considerable length with Dr. Pearse and representatives of the union. We discussed these very issues. I might say to the hon. member that nobody disagrees that the fleet, whatever shape it takes, will be smaller. In other words, the catching capacity simply has gone beyond the bounds of the potential of the biology. For that reason, we should not lose the opportunity to start reducing the size of the fleet. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. It is in the nature of a supplementary to a question asked a moment ago by my colleague from Hillsborough about equalization payments.
Business of the House
Is it the intention of the government to effect net savings in payments to the provinces under the new equalization formula? I understood the Minister of Finance to say that the answer to that would be no, but I would ask him to clarify that for me. If the answer is no, would he give a guarantee to the provinces which are eligible to receive equalization that they will receive no less than they would have received under the existing formula? If they do receive less, will the government make up the difference?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS EQUALIZATION PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
No, Madam Speaker, it is not possible to give that assurance. It has been demonstrated that the present formula for equalization is unworkable. The best proof of that is that in the course of this session it was necessary to bring in a special law in order to prevent Ontario from receiving equalization to which it was entitled under the equalization formula. Therefore, I would argue that a formula is defective if you have to exclude any particular province arbitrarily. That is why it was necessary to bring forward a new formula based on the Ontario standard, in the belief that the province of Ontario has the fiscal capacity to provide a reasonable standard of public service and that it is the job of equalization to ensure that all provinces have that reasonable standard. That is what we propose to do.
However, I would attempt to assure my hon. friend by telling him that, regardless of the change in the formula, the equalization payments for the first year of the new formula will increase by 15 per cent. I believe that is a rather substantial rate of growth in equalization payments that would occur to the provinces year over year.

1.	With reference to section 10.24 of the 1980 Report of the Auditor General, has the Canadian Pension Commission, since the release of the report, developed formalized standards for work processes within their control and (a) if so, what are they (b) if not, at what stage is the process?
2.	(a) Did the Department of Veterans Affairs consider setting down firm time guidelines for pension application processing and, if so, on what date will they be imposed (b) will there be self-imposed sanctions for failure to meet the guidelines and (i) if not, for what reason (ii) if so, what are they and will they help to shorten processing time periods?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. Bennett Campbell (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speechtext:
1. Section 10.118 of the 1980 Report of the Auditor General recommended that the Canadian Pension Commission formalize processing time standards, to the maximum extent practicable, in all areas of the pension adjudication process under its control. Formalized standards have not yet been developed.
(a)	Not applicable-see above.
(b)	A control system is now in operation which enables measurements of performance. Based on the information provided by this process control system, the commission is working towards establishing formal processing time standards to the extent practicable for those processes within its control.
2. (a) The commission has under consideration the establishment of time guidelines for processing pension applications. No firm date has been established for imposing such guidelines. The Auditor General has recognized that, because of the very wide variation between pension applications, the development of specific time guidelines for their processing may be virtually impossible. The commission is attempting to develop an over-all average target time for the processing of applications.
(b) Because each case is different, there can be no sanctions for not meeting an over-all average target date in individual cases. Over-all production will be closely monitored and appropriate action taken if the average target times are not met.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to thank hon. members for their courtesy in affording me the opportunity to speak at this time.
Last January when the aboriginal rights clause was first accepted by the constitutional committee, everyone present regarded it as a great step forward for the Indian, Inuit and Metis peoples of Canada. While joining in the general euphoria of the moment, at that time I said that members of the New Democratic Party would be looking very closely at
November 26, 1981

the amending formula for that section. Subsequently, the Leader of the New Democratic Party, the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), obtained a promise from the government that the aboriginal and treaty rights clause would be fully entrenched, as it was, in Section 55(c) of the resolution which was referred to the Supreme Court of Canada.
On Tuesday of this week the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) moved an amendment to include an aboriginal and treaty rights clause, but he did not include any formula for entrenchment or amendment. In the absence of any such formula the aboriginal people in the provinces are at the mercy of Section 42. Under that section those rights could be altered, amended or even extinguished by bilateral action of the federal government and individual provinces. Aboriginal rights in the Yukon and Northwest Territories could be altered or extinguished by the federal government acting unilaterally.
It is in this context that I wish to move an important amendment. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell):
That the motion of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development be amended by adding thereto after Section 35(2) the following:
35(3) An amendment to the Constitution of Canada in relation to the rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada set out in this part may be made by proclamation issued by the Governor General under the great seal of Canada only in accordance with the following procedure:
(a)	In the Yukon and Northwest Territories, when so authorized by resolution of a two-thirds majority vote in the Senate and House of Commons and with the consent of a majority of each of the aboriginal peoples so affected;
(b)	In the provinces, when so authorized in accordance with Section 41 and with the consent of a majority of each of the aborignal peoples so affected. (4) For the purposes referred to in Subsection 3 consent of the aboriginal
peoples shall be obtained by a procedure determined by the Government of Canada and the aboriginal peoples of Canada.
For the record, Mr. Speaker, the minister's amendment appears on page 40 of today's Order Paper.
In assessing the importance of this amendment and the need for it, let us begin by reviewing the process we have followed thus far. All of us remember that last October, when the constitutional resolution was first tabled in this House, there was a completely inadequate recognition of aboriginal and treaty rights. The Charter of Rights and Freedoms simply said that nothing would take away rights or freedoms that pertained to the native peoples of Canada. There was absolutely no positive recognition of what those rights might be.
We are aware of the Prime Minister's opposition to the recognition of aboriginal rights. In 1969 he said that, in his opinion, there was no such thing as aboriginal rights. The split decision of the Supreme Court of Canada regarding the case of the Nishgas in northern Brisith Columbia pointed out that there was very substantial legal opinion to the contrary, and he had to admit that maybe these people have more rights than he thought. As a result, the government came forward with a land claims policy but the narrow legalistic basis of this policy made it very difficult for many people to submit their claims and have them recognized.
The Constitution
In a memo submitted over the signature of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development there is a section entitled "Native Title Superseded by Law" which reads as follows:
It appears from an extensive historical and legal review that in settled areas of British Columbia, southern Quebec and Nova Scotia, native title has been superseded by law and as a consequence there is no basis under the 1973 policy for negotiating claims settlements in these areas.
This is the reality under which the native peoples have had to try to negotiate their settlements.
Last November I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) if it were not possible to have a clause put in the constitutional resolution that would recognize aboriginal and treaty rights. In his answer he indicated very clearly his own opposition to that kind of recognition.
It seems that the Prime Minister delights in the fact that not all Indian, Inuit and Metis leaders are in perfect agreement concerning rights. He is constantly using this as an excuse for refusing to deal honestly with their concerns, instead of taking a constructive leadership role in bringing these people together, helping them to sort out their priorities and major concerns which could perhaps mesh with the government's concerns. The Prime Minister has delighted in his role as lord of disunity.
In any event, the resolution was referred to the constitutional committee. At that time representatives of different bands, tribal councils and provincial and national organizations came before the committee requesting recognition and entrenchment of their rights. As I said earlier, the government heard and responded to those on January 30. It was a high moment for all people in that committee who were present when a clause was finally inserted into the constitutional proposal which recognized and affirmed the aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada.
However, the aboriginal peoples were not completely satisfied. They wanted a consent clause. It was not that they wanted Clause 34, as it was, to be removed from that proposal; rather, they wanted to go further. They wanted a clause stating that these rights could only be changed or amended with their consent. I ask, was their concern somehow un-Canadian, irrational or out of line?
In recent months we have seen that the provinces are very concerned about their role in the amending formula. The amending formula in the earlier constitutional proposal was acceptable to many hon. members in this House. We felt that it was fair and reasonably flexible. However, it was not acceptable to the majority of the provinces in 1981, even though it had been ten years earlier. Therefore, the provinces went back to the federal government. They lobbied and they got a different amending formula.
If it was right for the provinces to insist upon an amending formula acceptable to them, surely it was a legitimate act for the aboriginal peoples to insist on an amending formula which was acceptable to them and which would protect their rights.

The Constitution

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: DROITS DES PEUPLES AUTOCHTONES DU CANADA
speechtext:
The New Democratic Party has always supported and worked for such a clause. We would like to see that, and that is the purpose of our amendment today. The aboriginal people have no sound reason to trust their rights either to the federal or the provincial governments. They want and need all possible protection because they can look back on a history of 440 years of lies, deceptions and broken promises in Canada.
When Jacques Cartier kidnapped Donnacona and other Iroquois and took them to France, he began the long, unsu-cessful policy of trying to assimilate the Indian people. When he returned to Canada in 1541, all the Indians who had gone to France had died. Instead of admitting this, Cartier lied and told the other Iroquois that their relatives were living like lords in France and did not want to return. This was the first recorded lie to Canada's aboriginal people. It was the first lie, but absolutely not the last. A cynic might suggest that Jacques Cartier laid the two cornerstones of Canadian Indian policy: forced assimilation and lies.
I would like to give two recent examples showing why the Indian people feel they cannot trust the government. First of all, let us look at the question of the B.C. Indian cut-off lands. Back in the early years of this century, the British Columbia government and the federal government appointed a joint commission known as the McKenna-McBride commission to look into the size of Indian reserves in British Columbia. One of the important conditions was that no changes were to be made in the size of reserves without Indian consent. That was contained in the terms of reference. However, in actual fact thousands of acres of prime land were taken away without such consent, affecting 34 reserves and 22 bands in British Columbia. The government's position has been that this act was legal because it was done by legally formalized orders in council.
The Indian people have struggled for 60 years in an attempt to obtain justice on the B.C. cut-off lands issue, and it is still not resolved. That does not give them any confidence in either the federal government or the provincial government of British Columbia.
Second, we can recall that just a year and a half ago the Prime Minister promised that native leaders would be able to participate in first ministers' conferences in all matters directly relating to them. A section in the constitutional resolution was even tabled and sent to the Supreme Court of Canada last year, and it is still there in the present resolution. It states that native leaders, leaders of the aboriginal peoples, would be invited to the first ministers' conference to participate in discussions respecting constitutional matters which would directly affect the aboriginal peoples. That was the very explicit intent.
When the first ministers' conference was held earlier this month, where were the leaders of the aboriginal peoples. They were waiting in Ottawa. They asked to be present but they were not invited. They were not invited to the kitchen where
all the deals were made. They were not even invited to the main conference room to get a chance to state their case. As a matter of fact, there was no public discussion of aboriginal rights at that meeting. The only exception was Saskatchewan, which tabled a counter proposal including the aboriginal rights proposal.
Perhaps we get an idea of what went on when we look at British Columbia's attitude. The Premier of British Columbia first said that the aboriginal rights clause was left out by oversight and that it had not really been discussed at all. However, last week he said: "Yes, we would be willing to reinsert the aboriginal and treaty rights clause if the federal government were willing to pick up the costs". In other words, it all boils down to money. As far as the Social Credit government of British Columbia is concerned, the matter of human rights has a price tag on it.
Right now there are several land claims outstanding in British Columbia. In addition to the Nishga claim, there are the claims of the Gitskan Carrier band, the Kitwancool band, the Association of United Tahltans and the Haisla Nation. The land claims of all of these people have been accepted by the Office of Native Claims for negotiation, subject to provincial participation. However, the province has not indicated any willingness to participate. Other B.C. land claims from the Haida, the Heiltsuk and the Nuu Chalh Nhuh are awaiting word as to their acceptance and they will face the same stone wall attitude from the provincial government, which does not want to recognize aboriginal rights because it will cost money. It will take away from its revenue.
British Columbia and other provinces are worried about the costs of recognizing aboriginal rights. I submit that it is a proper part of their job. There is a price tag to the recognition of rights, and provinces, very naturally, must consider the cost. However, we must condemn the cynical attitude of Premier Bennett and the Social Credit government, as they would only consent to an aboriginal rights clause if the federal government were willing to pick up the tab. Certainly there is a price and we must consider it; but we also must consider the opposite, which is a denial of basic justice. Perhaps the government of British Columbia would remember the fact that it has benefited from the wealth of the land taken from the Indian people of British Columbia. Other governments and provinces have benefited from the land which has been taken.
It is now unacceptable to say that a government will only recognize rights if it can be scot-free of any expense. However, in a larger sense, I believe that we need to move beyond the question of cost. In addition to considering the costs of this program, we need to consider the possibilities. We should ask what contribution the aboriginal peoples of Canada can make to our society if we give them half a chance. What possibilities are there to enrich everybody's life if these people are enabled take their full place in Canadian society? Already they have made great contributions to our society, but they have been stymied and hemmed in by lack of resources and the denial of their rights.
November 26, 1981

In concluding, I simply want to remind all hon. members of the importance of this act of patriation. I want to remind hon. members that the relationship of the Crown to the aboriginal peoples of Canada is a relationship that predates the relationship of the federal government to the provincial governments. It is important, therefore, that this relationship be placed on a sound basis within our Constitution. If we do not do that, we will have a Constitution that is tainted. We will have a Constitution that has written into it a denial of basic justice.
It was good to see what happened last week when people demanded that aboriginal rights be put back into the Constitution. However, we would have been happier if the word "existing" had not been included. But even more than that, we want to see protection of those rights and we want to see those rights guaranteed to the Indian people, the Metis people and the Inuit people of Canada with an amending formula that protects them and is not at the mercy of unilateral action by the federal government or at the mercy of bilateral action by the federal government and one provincial government. We want to see an amendment which gives these people a say in the continuation of their rights and any change contemplated to their rights.
I urge all hon. members to join members of our party in supporting this very important amendment.

subtopic: DROITS DES PEUPLES AUTOCHTONES DU CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I begin to speak on the amendment to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly), 1 must say to members of the House that this is quite a way to write a Constitution.
We have here a proposal. I am not trying to reflect on the member's intentions; I know the hon. member and I believe his intentions are honourable, but it is difficult, in debating the Constitution, to address this issue and be able to resolve it in half an hour or less. The cudgel sort of hangs over our head that if we cannot do it in half an hour or less, then we better get on to the next issue. That is just not the way to write a Constitution.
Frankly, I abhor the way this is being done. It is not fair to the people-not to members of the House because that is by the by, so to speak. I suggest that we spend a little more time and thought on a Constitution that Canadians will have to live and work with in the future. My comments will be made with that in mind.
It almost reminds me of the kind of situation that took place in the constitutional committee. We would have a proposal put to us and within five minutes we were supposed not only to debate the merits of it but also declare them. What we did, which I think was acceptable to all members of the committee, was to put forward our whole body of amendments. Then members could look at them over a period of time, they could get back to their caucuses, discuss them and come up with rational debate as to the merits or lack thereof on any given issue.
Again I say to the hon. member that in making my comments I am not in any way trying to reflect on his method, it was the only avenue he had. But I suggest to him and to all members of the House that what he suggested is not the best way to approach this whole question. I am not talking about the native questions but rather the matter of Constitutionmaking.
Having said that, the subamendment of the honourable member has a number of aspects in it which I believe go directly to the heart of the accord. That creates difficulties for all members of this House who want to see the accord preserved and eventually the final vote taken. The subamendment provides, following the salutation:
In the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, when so authorized by resolution of a two-thirds majority vote in the Senate and House of Commons-
I will just stop there for a minute. The amending formula in the resolution that is before us, specifically Section 37(1), sets out the procedure for amending the Constitution of Canada, which is not a two thirds majority in the House of Commons or in the Senate. What is needed is a resolution of the Senate and the House of Commons, which I take to understand to mean 50 per cent plus one. That, I believe, is how this section is being interpreted. Yet for this purpose, and for this purpose only, there is to be a two thirds majority. That is simply

November 26, 1981
The Constitution
inconsistent with the resolution before us and the agreement that was made between the nine provinces and the Prime Minister of Canada. In that sense I do not believe we can accept the words "a two thirds majority". That is inconsistent with the accord before us.
Additionally, if we take a look at the honourable member's proposed Section 35(3)(a), after the words "of a two thirds majority vote in the Senate and House of Commons" it goes on to say:
-and with the consent of a majority of each of the aboriginal peoples so affected-
During the time that I held the responsibility of minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development-I see the honourable member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) is in the House and I know that he worked in the same way-we worked with the definition "the peoples involved". That was always difficult to determine. Who were the aboriginal peoples when you got down to the issue of, say, land claims? When you take a look at that section, Mr. Speaker, what would be the result? Consent of the majority of the peoples, that is the aboriginal peoples, but that leaves out the other peoples who live in those territories. While I have no difficulty personally in saying that the aboriginal peoples should be consulted, land claims only in those territories goes beyond just affecting the aboriginal peoples. These claims will affect the future of those territories and, therefore, the future and the lives of all people living in those territories.
If I could just give a practical example, Mr. Speaker, at the present time negotiations for a Yukon land claim are under way. I am pleased that those negotiations are going well. While the negotiations directly involve the Government of Canada and the aboriginal peoples of the Yukon through the umbrella of the Council of Yukon Indians, the legislative assembly of the Yukon, while not being directly involved in the decision-making in the negotiations, is an integral part of the negotiations. Everyone in the Yukon knows that if that land claim is to be successful it will require an agreement. By that I do not mean a formal agreement but a mental agreement or an understanding that in fact the land claim will be to the benefit not only of the aboriginal peoples of the Yukon, but will represent another step forward in reaching the possibility of the Yukon taking its rightful place in the Canadian family.
With all due respect to the hon. member, I see some real difficulties that will be created, not only for the Yukon at this time but as well for the Yukon and the Northwest Territories in the future. While there is an aboriginal majority in the Northwest Territories which, by the way, is reflected in the legislative assembly of the Northwest Territories, problems will exist in terms of the definition of who aboriginal peoples are; and that was a factor, for example, in the COPE agreement in principle. There was a problem there.
There is a problem, for example, in that people who are living in the Northwest Territories who are covered by the COPE agreement in principle are the beneficiaries of the
Alaska claim. I am not trying to say these people are not entitled under these claims, but I am trying to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, and to all members of this House, that this amendment goes very deeply to the natural development and evolution that is now taking place in Canada north of 60. We are deeply concerned that we are almost inserting ourselves into the centre of that process by this amendment.
I said I would not be long, Mr. Speaker, and I do not want to take advantage of the patience the House has shown on these issues, but if you look at Section 41, to which the second part of the amendment refers, you will see that the amendment states in part:	<
In the provinces, when so authorized in accordance with Section 41 and with the consent of a majority of each of the aboriginal peoples so affected-
I will not deal with the last part relating to the aboriginal peoples so affected, but Section 41 relates in part to the creation of new provinces; that is, the extension of the boundaries of the existing provinces and the creation of new provinces in the territories. It is the opinion and position of our party that we should go back to the position of 1871.
If you look at the resolution before us, Schedule I, the amendments of 1871, you will see that all that the resolution before us does is change the citation of the 1871 amendment. What it leaves in place is that the creation of new provinces in the territories shall be under the jurisdiction and responsibility of the federal government. That is why, when the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) and other members of our party speak later on, we want to refer back to Section 41(e) and (f), and that is why we would like to see those parts taken out. If we were to vote for this amendment we would in fact be voting against that principle; that is, that we feel this matter should fall within federal jurisdiction rather than a shared jurisdiction between the federal government and the provinces of Canada.
Lastly, if you will just bear with me for one more minute, Mr. Speaker, if one goes back to the point the hon. member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands made-and he made a valid point when the talked about the aboriginal people feeling frustration in the sense that they had not received the rights they felt they had been given-you will note his reference to the cut-off lands in British Columbia. I want to tell him that during the time I had responsibility as minister we tried to get also question of those cut-off lands resolved. Quite frankly, I thought we had almost done so, but I regret this still has not been accomplished. I sincerely believe it was just a matter of pushing this over the side, so to speak, and getting it done. I agree with the member that it has to be done and it should have been done. However, with all respect, I do not see how his amendment would necessarily speed up that process at this stage. I think there has to be moral suasion on the part of all of us to encourage that kind of agreement.
Moving now to Section 36, which calls for a federal-provincial conference to be participated in by the federal government, the provincial governments and the aboriginal peoples, Section 36(2) reads:
The conference convened under subsection (1) shall have included in its agenda an item respecting constitutional matters that directly affect the aborigi-
November 26, 1981

nal peoples of Canada, including the identification and definition of the rights of those peoples to be included in the Constitution of Canada, and the Prime Minister of Canada shall invite representatives of those peoples to participate in the discussions on that item.
I know, with all the history we have that has taken us to this point, that an argument can be made as to whether the native peoples were treated fairly. I think hon. members in this House have expressed the belief that they were not. We are now at the point where we have this provision in the resolution, and quite frankly good faith has to prevail. What is needed is that definition which is called for in that item on the proposed agenda of that conference, and which I suggest is also called for by the hon. member's amendment. 1 have pointed out that there will be difficulty when this conference starts this defining process, and it will take time.
I spoke to some native people yesterday and pointed out that while I accept the argument that wrongs have been done in the past-and I frankly do not think members of this House want to be party to more wrongs-it is now incumbent upon native leaders, the federal government, provincial governments and members of this house to put together an agenda for that conference whereby not only will the definition be discussed but it will finally be concluded. We must take time to do that adequately and properly.
If I could issue one warning to the federal government, it would be this. I see that conference taking place with the federal government acting not only as chairman, but also as a participant, taking its responsibilities under Section 91(2)(iv) as trustee. This will leave the aboriginal peoples to make their claims not only to the provinces, but to the federal government. The federal government will be there not only in the role of chairman, but also as defending the rights of the aboriginal peoples, fulfilling the responsibilities every federal government has had to accept.
That is how 1 interpret Section 36, and while I commend the hon. member for the sincerity I believe he had in putting forward the subamendment, I suggest not only is it premature but that it also violates the Accord; and, frankly, I think it could do more damage than good in terms of present negotiations.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PUBLICATION OF OPINION POLL RESULTS
speechtext:
that Bill C-262, to amend the Canada Elections Act (publication of the result of opinion polls), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is certainly not the first time I have brought a bill before this House on this particular subject. As a matter of fact, it is at least the sixth time that this particular bill has been before Parliament in my name and has been debated. Prior to that, other hon. members in this House had felt the same way I feel about the publication of polls during election campaigns.
On one occasion, the government did take some specific action. My bill, and also one standing in the name of another hon. member were referred to the broadcasting committee, where we had a very long and useful discussion. At that time the committee came in with a recommendation that action be taken by the government which would eliminate the publication of opinion polls during actual election campaigns. The government did not move on that recommendation.

What I hope we might accomplish today, as far as this particular piece of legislation is concerned, is that it be referred to the appropriate standing committee of the House of Commons. The committee could then discuss the matter and come forth with a decision, expressing its views in relation to the matter of polls. If there were a supportive view from that committee regarding the banning of the publication of polls during election campaigns, appropriate legislation to put it into effect might then be forthcoming from the government.
At this moment, the only province in Canada which bans the publication of public opinion polls during election campaigns is the province of British Columbia. I have often used the example of the election of the Bennett government in British
Columbia which was predicted by no one because there were no polls to give guidance to the great fourth estate in coming up with conclusions.
However, that is only one example, and it is not the reason I believe public opinion polls should be banned from public discussion during election campaigns. What really gives me great concern is not the actual raw information which comes from polls, but the pollution resulting from experts on the media who speak only about numbers and never about issues during election campaigns. They put people into the position of playing numbers games, wondering who is ahead and who says who is ahead.
The greatest travesty of poll results which has ever been perpetrated upon the public was evident in the last election campaign in the United States. Pollsters in that country were on every network of radio and television, and reported in every newspaper one could imagine. They told the people of that country that the election between Ronald Reagan and President Jimmy Carter would be a cliff-hanger, too close to call, with less than 1 per cent dividing the opinions of the public. On election day, the end result was that the people in California did not have to bother going to the polls because the election was over before they even got there. For instance, the ABC network carried out a raw poll almost as soon as the TV debate was concluded. The poll stated more than just who the public felt was the winner of the debate; it stated that Ronald Reagan was the people's choice. However, even with all of this evidence, on November 3, the day before the election, the public was told that it was a toss-up, with Ronald Reagan one point ahead of Jimmy Carter. As it turned out, Ronald Reagan was not one point ahead of Jimmy Carter the next evening, he was nine points ahead. Even with all of the protectors the pollsters put into their predictions, they cannot, in justice, explain away the misdirection they gave to the United States public.
While I have never suggested the art of polling should be banned, nor that politicians and political parties should be deterred from using them at any time, I believe more strongly than ever that from the date an election campaign officially begins until it is finished, there should be no polling information made available to the public. What a change it would be for the electorate to make decisions based on leadership and programs rather than percentages!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PUBLICATION OF OPINION POLL RESULTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PUBLICATION OF OPINION POLL RESULTS
speechtext:
For years John Diefenbaker said that polls were for dogs, and they knew best how to use them. That is part of the truth. Winston Churchill also had a very low opinion of polls. He said, "Oh that God would deliver us from the opinion polls; if only people would make decisions on rightness and wrongness rather than public opinion". And so right he was.
An illustration of my concern is what happened to us in the last general election. My leader, the right hon. member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), phoned me during that campaign because he knew I had spoken out against the publication of polls. He sought my assurance that I would reintroduce the
November 26, 1981

bill, as I had on many occasions in the past, because of the atrocities being committed against our party by all the instant experts in the media who knew what would happen. Of course, even in that election campaign, it did not happen.
In a country as mixed up as Canada, considering the different political persuasions of people in various regions, the publication of opinion polls could create terrible aberrations in poll results. For instance, in the last election campaign, where 74 Liberal members were elected in the province of Quebec, polling something like 70 per cent of the popular vote, how could one put that mix into a national poll and get any kind of a realistic assessment of what is happening in the country? One could not.
I was impressed with the fact that during the election campaign the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), himself, although I do not know his exact words, indicated his unhappiness with the manipulation of poll results to favour the instant experts who were telling the people what the results meant. We should really want to get down to discussing the democratic issues. The newspapers might jump on us and say we are trying to infringe on the freedom of the press if we prevent publication of poll results.
However, for one reason or another, people believe pollsters to be experts concerning what is happening, what will happen, how people will vote and how they think in the country. They sit there and talk about what is going on. I remember one election which was very close, I think it was the 1972 election. The CBC put on a program and brought all of its people from across the country. This was done after all advertising had been banned. The program went on the national network. There was no chance for our party to say anything and our party suffered on that particular occasion. These so-called experts from the CBC were polled. Without exception they stated that the Liberal government would be re-elected with a majority. They were all wrong. The government was re-elected but it won a minority and not a majority. There is no doubt in my mind that the intrusion by the media on that program into that election campaign had a major impact on the people who were still uncommitted and still in doubt. There were many doubts in that election campaign.
I do not think there is infringement on the freedom of the press if polls are banned. Instead, the banning of polls will force the reporters, who are being paid to write, is write stories about what is really happening in the country. These reporters will have to go out and do their job rather than rely upon numbers that are produced by one polling organization or the other as to how people are thinking and feeling. Writing is a reporter's job. Reporters should not fall back on the Gallup poll or some other polling organization for the background information they need to write their story. They should be out there among the people finding out what the people think.
If we do not have numbers games and we do not have polls, people will have to be questioned on the issues. When people are questioned on the issues, maybe they will realize what
Opinion Polls
election campaigns are all about. If ever there was an example where issues were not in question, it was the February 1980, federal election campaign. You could not find the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). You could not find out what the policies of the government were going to be either. We know now what they are, but we did not know then and we could not find out. There was nothing to talk about in that election campaign. There was no real debate, but there would have been had it not been for the fact that every week a new poll was released saying that the Conservative Party was 20 points behind, or something like that. That is great encouragement to the public to support our party in a given election campaign!
The shoe, of course, can be on the other foot. The other party can be in the same situation. We would have a much more realistic election campaign if we did not have the interference and intrusion of public opinion polls being released ad infinitum throughout an election campaign. People never get down to the issues while discussing numbers.
I hope this House at the conclusion of this discussion will give some consideration to referring this bill to an appropriate committee of the House so that we can really take a look at what can be done. People who are concerned with the issues can come before the appropriate committee to express their views, whether in relation to the infringement of freedom or whether in relation to the misinterpretation that is given to figures and the way they are determined.
I hope other members will participate in this debate. I hope they will give support at least to referring this bill to the appropriate standing committee of the House.
Mir. Gilbert Parent (Welland): Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to participate in this debate. I might preface my remarks by telling hon. members who are in the House that it is not often that I agree with the hon. member for Cumber-land-Colchester (Mr. Coates) but in this case I do. If not for the same reasons, I do agree in principle that the people of Canada in some way can be misled by the pollsters if these pollsters desire to do that.
Some time ago in Toronto I served on a panel. To say that I was one of the more unpopular panelists because of my stand on polls goes virtually without saying. 1 do not think it is "un-Liberal", if you will, to take this position. Questions that are asked by pollsters many times are so tailored that any kind of response can be elicited.
What would happen to the democratic process if we simply governed by polls? What would be the net effect on the people of Canada? Would this take away all of the incentive and interest for them to look at the issues of the day? Would it preclude any necessity on their part to inform themselves so that they could make intelligent decisions?
I must say to my dismay that polls taken over the years have been remarkably accurate many times. I think it was the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester who pointed out that in the 1948 American election it was predicted that the Republican candidate would win over the Democrat candidate, but this proved incorrect. However, hon. members will remember

November 26, 1981
Opinion Polls
that in 1948 we did not have as much immediate coverage by television. We had radio and newspapers. But television has immediate impact. Television stations take polls immediately after a speech is delivered. This happened not too long ago when a presidential candidate delivered a speech. Instant reaction was portrayed and it was done before people could digest what had been said. The commentators on the spot said the people of the country think this and that. But what they had done was to take a sampling of a few thousand people out of millions of people across the country.
[ Translation]
And I believe also that with polls carried out in this way, Mr. Speaker, just about any question can be asked. Many times questions asked by pollsters are so tailored that a specific response can be elicited. So with this kind of tool in the hands of pollsters who want to prove a point, the media and private industries can make the public believe anything. And we do have polls. Last week, they held a poll on the Grey Cup game. The team representing Western Canada was supposed to win by some twenty points. After the game, we realized that the score had been a lot closer than the pollsters had wanted us to believe.

I do not believe it is accurate to say that people are not influenced by polls. It would be nice to believe that all of the people of Canada could take the time to inform themselves about the issues on which they should inform themselves, whether it be an election or anything else. The fact is that many times those polls can be so doctored, and I use that term advisedly, as to bring about virtually any point of view the people who are conducting the polls want.
We saw this in respect of the Constitution. One of the questions regarding the Constitution was very simple: "Do you think that the provincial governments and the federal government should agree on a Constitution?" Naturally everyone in Canada would like us all to agree about virtually everything all the time in order to get along and be good fellows. The way that was interpreted was that unless there was agreement we should not go ahead with the Constitution. My opinion from talking to people across Canada is that many people, indeed, were in favour of our proceeding with this constitutional debate.
It is my belief that polls make up the minds of some people in this country, or that some people can be led by polls. In that sense, if that is not a miscarriage of the democratic process, surely it is undue influence of the electorate. They should be able to make up their own minds.
Should we be concerned about the cost of these polls? The cost in terms of dollars is not really that important to me because these polls are conducted by private groups, people who indeed make their living conducting polls and peddling them to whoever wants to read them. One can get polls on virtually everything in this day and age. What about the cost
of polls when individuals virtually give up, if not their right, their desire to look into the fundamental issues that are being discussed? This cost in democratic terms is one which is unbearable in any democracy. Would we indeed become a government run by pollsters and, if so, why should the people of a constituency elect a Member of Parliament, a member of a legislative assembly or, indeed, a member of a municipal council if all we have to do is call 200 or 2,000 people at any given time and hold a poll to determine an issue? When these polls involve people who are not as informed as they should be, or people who react on emotion as opposed to thinking the process through, I suggest that the cost is the abrogation of the rights we have and that we must exercise as citizens.
Let me digress for just a bit because I think this has to do with polls. I want to make known my views on the amount of time we take for our elections. I believe the issues can be put forward to the people of Canada in a much shorter time than we now allow. It was suggested during a debate here last spring that perhaps we should have a standing list of voters across Canada rather than making up a list just before election time. I would prefer to have a shorter campaign period than we now have. I would suggest that four weeks from the time a writ is issued would be sufficient, in this day of instant communication across the country, for people to make up their minds.
The hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester said of the 1980 election that the people did not have a chance to bring forward the issues and discuss them thoroughly. I believe he said that "the Prime Minister could not be found". If he meant the Prime Minister of that time, I would agree with him because the then Prime Minister was a member of his own party. I guess we could say the same thing happened in 1979 when we did not have a vote for anyone, but rather a vote against certain things. Perhaps it could be said that people do not win elections, but that elections are lost for whatever reason.
I believe that polls, whatever they may be on, tend to be usurped by the media in order to get people excited. The hon. member pointed out that during the last election campaign the pollsters showed there was a 40-point spread between the parties. Did he say there was a 40-point spread between the parties? He suggested that because of this great spread-and I do not think it was that great-people tended to ask themselves why they should go out and work for the party or the candidate when the result had already been decided. I agree with the hon. member.
It is small wonder that at the last federal election we had 74 per cent or 75 per cent-shall I exaggerate-of the people of Canada exercise their franchise. Why would the people not come out and vote, exercising their democratic right in this country? Were they influenced by the pollsters to the extent they felt that this party was so far ahead and this one so far behind that they need not take the time to go out and vote, that it would mean nothing because the election had already been decided? The election had been decided then by whom?
November 26, 1981

Was it decided by the pollsters or by the media? I suggest that is unacceptable in a democratic society.
Let me point out also with regard to elections that 1 would personally be in favour of what they do in Australia. There, if you vote you get a certain tax rebate; I believe that is how they work it. If you do not vote, then whatever taxes you have to pay must be paid and there is no rebate at all. This encourages, and some would even say it forces, the people to get out and exercise their right to vote. This would give us a truer picture of the feelings of the people at the time of an election.
I am opposed to polls being published during an election campaign. My wish is that there would be no polls published from the time the writ is issued. We should have legislation on this particular matter. The matter should be studied by a committee. We should hear what the pollsters have to say about their part in the whole situation. I would ask that in the meantime, until we have legislation, the people who are involved in these polls-newspapers, television stations and research bureaux, wherever they are-should take the responsibility upon themselves to declare their own moratorium on the publication of poll, unless they really want to influence the people and not just report what the people are supposed to be thinking. If that were the case we would not run the risk of having government by pollsters rather than by the people through their elected Members of Parliament or their legislative assemblies.
I agree with the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester and I would urge that this bill be sent to committee, where there could be open and frank discussion by all the people concerned with these polls-the pollsters themselves, the people in public office and, indeed, people from the public at large. Then we could know what their views on the polls are and the effect they have on the voting process in Canada.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PUBLICATION OF OPINION POLL RESULTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too would like to say a few words about Bill C-262. I commend the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester (Mr. Coates) for bringing this discussion to the House today.
The whole question of polling is something which has bothered and intrigued me for many years. It seems to me in a general way that what has happened, perhaps unwittingly on the part of pollsters, is that over the years they have actually usurped the right of citizens to think for themselves. I am not saying that they have done this deliberately but I suspect that what has happened, particularly among those members of the voting public who are not constantly interested in politics and may be undecided at election time, is that they suddenly find themselves unconsciously influenced by polls. 1 think this perhaps relates directly to the herd instinct that is in all of us; that one wants to go with the winner. If a person has not followed a local or national campaign for three or four weeks and has not studied the issues, or has not watched the television or listened to radio or gone to an all-candidates meeting or read about candidates' views in the newspapers, it becomes very easy for an uncommitted voter or, perhaps, a disinterested
Opinion Polls
voter who nonetheless is a good citizen to sit back and say, "Well, John Brown or the leader of this or that party is ahead in the polls by 6 per cent" and instinctively there is the urge to go along with the winner and to be on the winning team without giving any serious consideration to the issues.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to hon. members in the House, that over the years the polls have both relieved people of the responsibility of considering election issues for themselves and, on the other hand, swayed people toward voting in a way they would not have otherwise voted had they taken more time to consider the issues, the candidates and the leaders.
I am speaking in support of Bill C-262. Another problem I find with polls is that they tend to focus on the leaders-not just on the substance of the individuals but on their appearance as it is portrayed on television, radio or in public. Polls tend to simplify, perhaps even oversimplify a leader's potential or actual capabilities. The reason for this is that people today are very easily influenced by television, the most intimate medium of all. In many cases, the very people who are conducting the polls are often closely connected to the various broadcast networks. I believe that this only adds to the confusion, because when people are asked on television a simple question, such as what do they think of Mr. X as leader of Y party, the immediate concern of that person is how he or she looks on television. The same can be said for radio. Of course, that poll can be greatly distorted, and when an uncommitted voter sees that a certain party is ahead nationally by two, four or eight points, that perhaps is not really the case.
To return to my first comment, a double error is made in judgment. The herd instinct takes over. The uncommitted voter may see that a certain party will win, so they might as well vote for that candidate in their constituency. I believe that polling, in general, distorts election campaigns. I believe it is unfair to all parties, particularly parties at the local level where a candidate may be running well ahead of his opponent, yet his opponent's party is deemed to be well ahead in a poll and the candidate who is ahead suffers as a result.
If the government will eventually have the courage to introduce legislation based on Bill C-262 and it is passed into law, I suppose that the media will be on our backs. The pollsters may not, but the media will cry foul. They will say that this prohibits or limits freedom of the press.
Well, both hon. members who have spoken before me, I think, have made very good arguments to refute this. This bill does not in any way limit freedom of the press or freedom of expression. In fact, as one hon. member pointed out, it will make the media work harder. It will have to cover a campaign in the good, old-fashioned way of 40 or 50 years ago when leading print journalists used to follow the leaders in this country, the United States and Europe on election campaigns. These journalists went to all the meetings and had the time during the evening or during the night, whether they were on trains or buses or in a hotel room, to think about what had been said. I think they were able to come to a much more

November 26, 1981
Opinion Polls
educated conclusion because they had a longer time to think about what had been said.
Now that we are in the electronic age, I hope that a bill such as Bill C-262 will make the media slow down a bit, because instant wisdom from television is getting out of control. If Bill C-262 is passed into law some day, the media people will have to think more and analyse more before they begin typing or "mouthing off', as we might say, on television and radio.
Polls tend to package elections into just too neat a form. They take away a lot of the natural and human element of an election campaign. Therefore, I suggest that this bill proposed by the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester should be given a great deal of consideration, and I hope it will be sent to the appropriate committee and that the government will act on the recommendations of that committee.
1 see one major problem which has nothing to do with the drafting of this bill, that is that Canada has 3,000 miles of border between it and the United States and approximately 70 per cent of Canadians live within 60 miles of the United States border. I do not know how we would be able to prevent American pollsters or anyone else from taking polls and either print the results or, worse, broadcast them on American radio and television networks. I do not know how we can get around that problem. I envision a lot of pirating and high profits being made by taking so-called non-professional, non-profit commercial polls. For example, university students could be used to do a poll which would then be relayed down to Buffalo or Rochester from where those results could be broadcast. The vast majority of Canadians who own television sets can easily watch American television stations or listen to American radio.
It is one problem that should be dealt with and, of course, it is part and parcel of the larger and more important problem vis-a-vis the influence of American television on Canada. With the exception of that loophole, which I hope and expect can eventually be tightened up with a tremendous amount of effort on our part, I highly commend this piece of legislation.
I understand that this is the sixth time that this bill has been debated in the House. The government has obviously seen fit to talk it out on the five previous occasions. I understand that this is probably what they are about to do today, and that is usually the name of the game in private members' hour.
However, I would like to urge government members who are opposed to this bill or its coming on stream now to seriously consider within their own caucus, and certainly within cabinet, to allow a bill such as this to come before the House in the name of the government, or a government minister for a free and open debate and then to go to committee.
The government may be surprised by the fact that there would be fairly widespread support for this bill. Perhaps we could even have a free vote on this bill. The only problem I can see, if my information is correct, is that, notwithstanding what the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Parent) said a few moments ago, the Liberal Party of Canada has relied very heavily on polls taken at election time. I do not know whether
those polls are commissioned by the Liberal Party of Canada. I do not know whether they spend money commissioning them. I suspect they do. Maybe I will be enlightened in a few minutes and the answer will be no.
If the Liberal Party of Canada is heavily dependent on these private and very expensive polls, I suggest to the Liberal members in the House that they try to bring back a little more democracy into our politics, reduce the influence of the electronic media in politics, give people at least the opportunity that their grandfathers had to think for themselves at election time and not be overwhelmed by a numbers game that is not always accurate.
I hope that in our lifetime this will reach cabinet, come into the House for debate and be passed into law. I am afraid that if we do not get a handle on the situation now, the electronic media in the country and throughout the western world will some day, without our even being aware of it, take over virtually the entire electioneering that goes on in this part of the world. They have far too much influence on the voters. It should be left to the candidates. If we goof and make a mistake, we pay for it at the polls. Let us not be pre-judged by these professional pollsters, let the people judge us on our merits.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PUBLICATION OF OPINION POLL RESULTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for the opportunity to participate in this debate and to support my colleague from Nova Scotia, the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester (Mr. Coates) who has presented Bill C-262 to the House for consideration. If I may begin where the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn) left off and point out that what we have for consideration is a reference of this bill to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. It is important that, if the House is not willing to consider the content of this bill in terms of passing it into law we at least take the opportunity to have the subject matter of the use of polls in relation to federal elections reviewed by a committee of the House.
We have in the debate to this moment heard from not only the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester, who represents the Progressive Conservative Party, but from the hon. member for Welland representing the Liberal Party and the hon. member for Brant representing the New Democratic Party. They all agree there is some real merit to the proposal. It is very difficult, in light of the expressions of that all-party support, to have the bill simply talked out so that it will no longer be considered in the House or committees of the House. I intend to yield the floor in sufficient time to allow the motion to refer Bill C-262 to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections to be put to a vote.
Let me begin my remarks on Bill C-262 by referring to the principle that it involves. It involves the very important matter of freedom of speech and freedom of communication. We have before us at the present time the constitutional proposal. In that proposal as part of the Constitution Act, 1981, which the House will be asked to approve and enact into law through the
November 26, 1981

Parliament of the United Kingdom, there is a statement of fundamental freedoms. Section 2 of the Constitution Act reads:
Everyone has the following fundamental freedoms:
(a)	Freedom of conscience and religion;
(b)	Freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression, including freedom
of the press and other media of communications;
There is no question that across this nation the freedom to express one's views is of prime importance, but that has to be considered in the context of the real world. We recognize immediately that there are qualifications put on that freedom of expression and freedom of communication.
We have already recognized in a myriad of provisions in the Canada Elections Act that, in relation to a political campaign, there is not entirely freedom of expression in the ultimate sense of that concept; in particular, as other hon. members have pointed out, there are already restrictions on advertising. Candidates who seek elected office must indicate in their advertising the source of that advertising, who sponsored it and other forms of identification. There is a ban on advertising in the period immediately preceding an election. Under the Canada Elections Act, elections advertising is banned prior to the date of the election being announced. Therefore, we have it established clearly that there are already existing limitations on communication. I do not think any member of the House or any person in Canada would regard these limitations as unreasonable.
The hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester is asking the House to consider another restriction, a restriction which, in the opinion of the hon. member, as he so aptly expressed it in his speech when presenting this bill today, will advance in the ultimate the freedom of choice which all citizens ought to be able to exercise in a federal election.
The balancing of rights is the matter which the House has to consider in this and other measures that come before it. On one hand we have the right as citizens to freely express ourselves in the course of an election campaign and, on the other hand, the need to protect the secrecy of the ballot, and the need to allow all citizens to make an appropriate and proper choice in an election campaign.
This bill recognizes that the use of polls during an election campaign becomes an impediment in the exercise of free choice of the citizen to vote and exercise his or her franchise. How can that occur? That is to say, how can it come about that a citizen is impeded in the exercise of his or her free choice in an election campaign?
You learn something from time to time by listening to members debate in the House. In the course of his remarks, the hon. member for Welland came up with an excellent phrase, "undue influence". The phrase "undue influence" has been in the law for years. We recognize that concept in the matter of will-making. It is said that a testator who makes a will must have free choice and not be subjected to undue influence. Undue influence can be exercised by persons pressing the testator at the time he is making a will and influencing him to leave his property in a certain way or subject to certain
Opinion Polls
conditions. For centuries the law has said that if that kind of influence is exercised, the will should not be valid because it is not the act of the maker of the will. He would have been subject to undue influence.
That is what we are talking about when we support a measure such as the one contained in Bill C-262; namely, the use of polls in the election campaigns in the current environment becomes an undue influence, unduly influencing voters.
As I indicated, there are many ways in which a voter can be influenced in an election campaign. For example, we recognize that a voter might be influenced by the manner in which votes were cast in an advance poll. In some cases an advance poll is taken two weeks prior to an election. The results are not announced until polling day. Why not simply count the votes when the advance poll closes and make an announcement? The reason must be that this might improperly influence voters on polling day.
If a poll taken on a scientific base is an accurate indication of the view of the persons polled who constitute the voters in an election, that would act as a similar influence on the voters. Assuming it is accurate, it would not be unlike announcing the result of an advance poll which, of course, is prohibited under the Canada Elections Act. If one were to make the analogy between the advanced poll and the poll taken under scientific conditions, one would have the answer: The voters should not be given this kind of information because, similarly to announcing the result of the advance poll, it may act unduly to influence voters in an election campaign. That is one of many arguments that can be made.
To give some background to the matter, Mr. Speaker, we should consider polls as they are constituted at present. In past years, polls were really guess work. I think that is where the expression "straw polls" came from. It meant you threw straws into the air and judged the result by how and where the straws landed. Since then, Mr. Speaker, polls have been conducted on a more scientific basis. As a result of efforts of social scientists and statisticians, over the years, a reasonably accurate, in some cases a tremendously accurate method has been established for determining what people will do in certain circumstances. It not only applies to the electoral process, but it applies to a great many other things. Many manufacturers in marketing their product rely on information obtained from polls. I think it has been established fairly clearly, Mr. Speaker, that the scientific technique has been developed to the stage where polls can be very accurate.
It is quite possible and conceivable that individuals in Canada would take a poll result as being a definite indication of the outcome of an election. You may say, Mr. Speaker, what is wrong with that? Again, I think it disturbs the freedom of choice in an election campaign. It is the kind of interference with the principle and concept of the secrecy of the ballot. For example, one should not be allowed to look into the ballot box to see how the person who came before you voted, and at the same time one should not be given informa-

November 26, 1981
Opinion Polls
tion that may amount to the same thing; that is, one has advance notice or a preview of what will be the election count.
As I have said, the matter before the House is not simply the passage of the provision proposed by Bill C-262, which is the prohibition of the publication of polls during an election campaign, but, more important, it is the reference of this subject to a committee of the House. We do not have to decide the matter today; we merely have to decide whether the matter should be further explored. I think that is very important in the light of the scientific developments that have taken place. In a very short time, Mr. Speaker, polls will advance to the stage where people will regard them as a true and accurate indicator of an election result. I believe and suspect this is already happening.
In a recent election in Nova Scotia, in some cases poll results were announced that indicated one candidate was well ahead in the election campaign. In fact, when the polling day arrived, that candidate trailed another candidate by a considerable number of votes. I happened to be very involved in that election campaign, and I firmly and honestly believed that the publication of a poll did affect the outcome of our particular election.
The next question is to determine whether that is good or bad. The supporter of the candidate, of course, who eventually won that election, would think it is a good thing. Other persons would disagree with that. I happen to be one who disagrees with that.
In exercising the franchise in that particular constituency, I believe that the voters were influenced by that particular poll. Why am I mentioning this in the Parliament of Canada? It is because it subsequently came to light that the poll was not as accurate as it purported to be. In fact, it purported to be a scientific poll that was conducted under the auspices of a university professor who utilized his students in a particular statistics course. Subsequently I spoke with one of the students and was told that it was nothing of the kind, that the students were simply given the assignment of selecting persons and coming back with the results of their particular survey. Those results were tabulated and the total result was established and communicated. The reason Parliament should consider this matter, Mr. Speaker, is that it is the broad public concept that polls are now accurate, and that once that concept becomes recognized by the public, unscrupulous people will take advantage of that faith and will attempt to manipulate polls in such a way that it will affect the outcome of an election. That is reason enough to have this matter considered in Parliament.
Very recently-in fact, a few weeks ago-I had the opportunity to appear as a guest before the student parliament in Halifax, the Halifax-Dartmouth Regional Student Parliament. Interestingly enough, the topic of debate that day was the publication of polls. I had the opportunity to hear both sides of the question expressed very well. I noted that the students grasped very quickly the element of freedom of speech that is involved in this particular question and, at the same time, the need for sensible restrictions on the right to express and communicate freely to Canadians. When I addressed the
participants in that parliament afterwards, I could not help saying that I had considered the matter, as they had, and had come to the conclusion that in that particular situation, and bearing in mind the developments that had taken place, the balance had swung, in my view, in favour of at least considering the banning or prohibiting of the publication of polls during an election campaign, for some of the reasons 1 have just outlined. In my area we have a radio station called CFDR that has acquired what is known in the trade as a telephone computing device. That telephone computing device has been used to take polls in election campaigns. The results of the polls taken by that particular station have been communicated and published, particularly when the polls have supported a particular party. I will not draw any inferences, but I will say that the principal shareholder, the president, director and managing operator of that station, is none other than C. Arnold Patterson, who was press secretary to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) for some months and who today is before the CRTC applying for another licence to operate a television station in the Halifax area.
If I had no other reason for wanting this matter to be considered by Parliament with a view to banning the publication of polls during an election campaign, there would be sufficient reason in that one instance. Here we have a political partisan who apparently owns a radio station, who has control of poll taking machinery and who publishes the results of that poll at his whim and at his desire.
Let me end my remarks so that we can vote on this issue by referring, as did the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester, to the words of the Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker. Mr. Diefenbaker said on many occasions that "the only poll that counts is the poll taken on election day". I believe we will preserve the dignity and the good sense of that remark by having this matter considered and banning the publication of polls in the manner suggested by my good friend.
