subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-PROCESSING OF APPLICATIONS FOR DISABILITY PENSIONS. (B) TERMS OF ELIGIBILITY
VETERANS AFFAIRS-PROCESSING OF APPLICATIONS FOR DISABILITY PENSIONS. (B) TERMS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 5 I directed a question, which appears at page 12533 of Hansard, to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Campbell) concerning the recent War Veterans Allowance Board decision that expanded the definition of the term "theatre of war", to include areas such as Newfoundland and Jamaica, thereby making previously ineligible veterans pensionable for war veterans allowance purposes.
I asked the minister whether the government would give consideration to broadening further the terms of eligibility for pension benefits to include those veterans who, through no fault of their own, were stationed in Canada during the war and were not given the opportunity to serve overseas and up to now have not been eligible for pension.
I thought perhaps the minister's answer was somewhat vague. He felt sure that the War Veterans Allowance Board would continue to look at ways and means of further extending those benefits to other veterans. Does this mean that the department will eventually recognize the valuable service of veterans stationed in Canada by extending pension benefits, and that it is just a matter of time before those veterans receive pensions?
I would suggest that veterans should not have to wait until the War Veterans Allowance Board is inclined or disposed to extend benefits. I believe the minister should take steps, through amending existing legislation, so that these veterans who would have gladly gone into front line service if called upon will receive the pensions they so rightly deserve. A change in legislation is what veterans need. So I ask the minister to do everything possible to introduce legislation to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act, and as soon as possible.
There is another area of concern to our veterans I should like to mention to the minister at this time. I refer to those World War II veterans taken prisoner in Hong Kong who contracted the parasite strongyloidosis. I hope the minister will give serious consideration to the adverse and long-lasting effects this parasite has had on veterans when looking at their applications for pensions.
Long delays in processing claims for benefits are another major concern of veterans. The hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) has brought this matter to the attention of the House before, that is, the serious delays veterans face when applying for pensions to which they are rightfully entitled. These points are major and pressing, and they are concerns expressed by veterans' associations. We all believe these concerns are very well founded.
I realize that the Minister of Veterans Affairs has only recently been elected to the House of Commons and that it
does take all of us a bit of time when first elected to get the feel of things around there. I feel confident, therefore, that the minister will be looking into those problems I have mentioned and will redress as soon as possible the injustices and inequities to all concerned veterans.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. Bennett Campbell (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-PROCESSING OF APPLICATIONS FOR DISABILITY PENSIONS. (B) TERMS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) has in fact raised three questions. He realizes I only have two and a half or three minutes to respond, so maybe I could address the question he raised initially, that is the question of the recent decision by the War Veterans Allowance Board to expand the benefits of war veterans allowance to those veterans who served in Newfoundland.
This involves, of course, not a change in legislation but merely a change in interpretation, in that it has been determined that veterans who were transported beyond the territorial waters of North and South America and the adjacent islands while on duty were considered to have served in a theatre of war. This ruling is merely, as you know, an expansion of the previous definition of "theatre of war" for the purpose of the War Veterans Allowance Act. This expansion of eligibility was possible within the criteria which are set out in existing legislation.
As I mentioned in response to the question from the hon. member, with the exception of those who served in both world wars and those who suffered some pensionable disability as a result of service during either war, the act requires that a veteran has served in an actual theatre of war to be eligible for an allowance. The Board continues to review all areas of service in order to ensure that all those who served in areas of war or theatres of war be given full access to the benefits of war veterans allowance.
On the other hand, in order to extend eligibility to those persons who served in Canada only during either wars, a change to the legislation would be required. That, Mr. Speaker, raises the question, as I mentioned in my answer to the hon. member, whether such a change would be acceptable, considering it would be contrary to the legislation as originally envisaged. It has always been considered that those who did serve in a theatre of war may have been affected in ways which are not readily apparent on medical examination. Therefore, those veterans have always been in a special category recognized by the Government of Canada.

subtopic: HAZARDOUS SUBSTANCES-UREA FORMALDEHYDE FOAM INSULATION-COMPENSATION SOUGHT FOR HOME OWNERS
HAZARDOUS SUBSTANCES-UREA FORMALDEHYDE FOAM INSULATION-COMPENSATION SOUGHT FOR HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for many months now we on this side of the House have been trying to get answers from the government on the urea formaldehyde foam insulation crisis. I use the word "crisis"
November 26, 1981

advisedly because over the past few weeks especially, this UFFI mess has been developing into a monster of staggering proportions, a result of a gargantuan blunder by this government going back to the mid to late 1970s.
The mind boggles at the number of unanswered questions which only serve to raise more questions, more fears on the part of Canadians who were encouraged to instal urea formaldehyde foam insulation by the government, who were then warned by this same government that the substance might constitute a health hazard, who were then told that the foam was officially banned for health reasons by the government, and who now find that the government cannot appear to get its act together and come up with some positive answers, some hope, some way out of the predicament that it has put these home owners into in the first place.
The government officially banned urea formaldehyde foam insulation a year ago. What has happened since? The government has left hundreds of thousands of people hanging out to dry by ducking questions or running off in six different departmental directions. We have heard the latest chapter just in the last few days, that of lending and banking institutions becoming twitchy in terms of renewing mortgages for people who have UFFI in their homes.
I am glad to see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. McCauley) in the House this evening. I do not envy him trying to answer some of the questions that are weighing so heavily on the minds of some half a million Canadians. But still, Mr. Speaker, I must put these questions to him because it is the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) who acts as the government's umbrella spokesman on the UFFI crisis. The problem is that so far in the House, his umbrella has brought nothing but more bad luck to those with foam in their homes.
I cannot believe the previous answers that the minister has given in the House that it is not the Canadian government's fault that home owners used these products in the first place or that the government must not accept the blame now. Much of the blame, says the minister, lies with the provinces.
Therefore, one question I hope the parliamentary secretary will answer tonight is how the government can use the provinces as a scapegoat for this UFFI mess. The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which granted acceptance numbers for the foam's national use, is not provincial. The Canadian Home Insulation Program, CHIP, which promoted and paid Canadians to instal the foam with CMHC's approval, is not provincial. Health and Welfare Canada, which studied, then temporarily banned, then permanently banned the material, is not provincial. Energy, Mines and Resources and Consumer and Corporate Affairs officials who refused to recommend UFFI and, indeed, cautioned against its use, are not provincial.
Adjournment Debate
I hope the parliamentary secretary will not repeat the line that the provinces have to share a great deal of the blame for this mess and that Ottawa is not responsible, because if you can believe that, you will believe that Colonel Khadafy just graduated from the Dale Carnegie School of Public Relations.
While we are on the involvement of CHIP, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that the government start preparing lists of those homes financed under the CHIP program so that we can have exact numbers and addresses, and that these numbers and addresses of every home insulated under CHIP are available. This is imperative so that if, as, and when the government decides on compensation for those who need to remove the foam and then restore homes to their original condition, people will not have to wait another six months or so.
Let me come to another very serious dimension to this UFFI problem-one of the questions which must be answered- which has come to light only in the past 24 hours. We know that anywhere from 80,000 to 100,000 homes are affected in one way or another by UFFI. What about apartments? In its investigation of the UFFI matter, has the government considered the number of apartment buildings which may have foam in them? I know of at least two large apartment complexes where the presence of UFFI has been detected and indeed verified.
One tenant watched the foam being blown into his apartment building about three years ago. He began suffering a scratchy throat and put a humidifier in his apartment. When UFFI was banned, he went to his property manager to ask if the foam was in the building. When he got an evasive answer, he had the health department team in to test his apartment. The reading was just a touch below the federal Health and Welfare Department's proposed safety level. He informed the apartment owner, asked if any other tenants in that apartment building had testing done, and was told to keep his mouth shut and not inform the other tenants.
I have passed along the particulars of this situation in confidence to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and to the provincial ministry of health in Toronto. I do not feel it is fair to alarm other tenants in that building or to have them harassed. I only use this example to indicate that the UFFI program may yet be reaching a magnitude that not even this government is aware of.
I want to make one final point in this short presentation. Of course, not everyone who has UFFI in their homes or maybe apartment buildings will have problems, not now anyway. Nobody knows whether there could be cumulative effects down the road. It is the uncertainty, the fear of the unknown, the fact that this government, which has known about the UFFI problem for so long, has been offering precious little hope to Canadian home owners. Hope starts with positive information. That is what we need. I hope, on behalf of all

November 26, 1981
Adjournment Debate
those people we have been meeting across this country and who have been writing to my office, that positive information is what we get, beginning tonight, from the parliamentary secretary.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gary F. McCauley (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: HAZARDOUS SUBSTANCES-UREA FORMALDEHYDE FOAM INSULATION-COMPENSATION SOUGHT FOR HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to respond to my good friend and colleague in the House, the hon. member for Hamilton Wentworth (Mr. Scott), whose admirable rhetoric sometimes gets in the way of the facts. I want to take this opportunity to set the record straight with respect to government initiatives relating to urea formaldehyde foam insulation. From the outset, this government has acted responsibly and speedily on this issue to ensure that the health of Canadians is protected.
Prior to November 1979, less than a handful of health-related complaints had been registered with the government against this product. An interdepartmental committee was set up to examine this issue in response to information emanating from other jurisdictions, namely the United States of America.
By September 1980 the government had received approximately 100 complaints, and an advisory committee of health experts was organized to examine the issue and report to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin). Based on the recommendation of this committee, the government acted promptly and banned UFFI under the Hazardous Products Act.
Since that date of less than a year ago, the government has continued to act responsively to home owners who require assistance and information. On June 15, 1981, the UFFI Information and Co-ordination Centre was established by the government to provide information to the public, administer a national testing survey and co-ordinate federal efforts. A toll-free telephone system was set up, which to date has responded to over 10,000 inquiries.
A series of information booklets has been written and disseminated to thousands of individuals. Further publications are planned. Important and promising research is under way which touches upon the use of neutralizers, the effectiveness of remedial measures and the structural effects of UFFI on homes.
On August 24 of this year the government announced that 2,400 homes would be tested to determine formaldehyde gas levels, with special priority given to home owners reporting medical problems. This survey is now completed and an analysis of the results is under way.
Unfortunately, due to the restraints of time, it is impossible for me to touch upon all the elements and history of this problem. I do, however, wish to comment on a particularly important facet, and that is the board of review which was established under the Hazardous Products Act. This board is conducting public hearings into the safety, history and use of UFFI. Thousands of pages of testimony have been recorded
and over 250 exhibits have been filed. Hearings have taken place in Halifax, Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto, Calgary and Vancouver. The board has heard virtually any individual wishing to present evidence, including consumers, federal and provincial government officials and members of the business and professional communities. As can be readily seen, Mr. Speaker, the government has reacted quickly to this situation by putting in place a program that responds to this very complex issue. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) has stated on several occasions that the government must have available valid, scientific data on which any further government action can be based.
The formulation and analysis of this data is being actively pursued.

Mr. Speaker, on November 6, 1981, I asked a question of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). It dealt with the hours of work of railway employees, who have to work as much as eleven hours without rest. As reported in Hansard of November 6, 1981, at page 12599, the minister answered my question by saying:
-you and others would find me doing something that is not of my competence, of my jurisdiction.
I want to say that we are talking about the minister's jurisdiction. This is the second time I have asked this minister about this problem. Tonight I will try another approach. Tonight I will put the Minister of Transport on a unit on one of the Canadian railways. We will call the minister. He will be okay for duty. He will be waiting to be called to go to work. He could get up at eight o'clock in the morning and possibly wait six or eight hours to get his call. Finally, he will be called. He gets a two hour call. He will have his meal and then will go out to work. He will climb up on a unit, with one employee on the head-end and another one on the tail-end. His train could be anywhere from 10,000 to 14,000 tonnes. He will start on the way to his destination. I want to talk about the mountainous area. It could be snowing that evening. It could be snowing heavily when he starts out. He could be anywhere from the age of 40, 50, 60 or 65, as many of them are. He will start his journey on this train going through small communities. On this train he could be carrying dangerous commodities. He will be on that train for eight, nine or 10 hours. As the train gets going, we find it at the top of the grade, and there is a passenger train down the hill, with probably 500 passengers sitting down there waiting for this train to come. The minister will be watching the signals. Mind you, he will be on duty for ten hours, he will be on duty for unable to stop to eat because he must not delay his train. He will start down that grade. I will remind the
November 26, 1981

House of the fact that 500 passengers are sitting on the train. He has been on duty for ten hours. He is weary but his contract did not provide him with the opportunity to say, "I am tired". He has to carry on because the union agreement indicated that he must. The Minister of Transport has not brought in laws so that after eight hours he could say, "I am too tired, I cannot carry on." But the passengers have no contract. They are at his mercy. What about the small village down there all these explosives on the train? The people of the village do not have a contract.
The Minister of Transport has a responsibility to bring forward legislation which would indicate that an employee, after eight hours on duty, should be the judge of his own condition. It has nothing to do with the contract. It is only so that the employee can say he is not fit to carry on, or "I feel fine. It was only two or three hours. I feel good, I will take my train to its destination".
Surely the Minister of Transport has a responsibility to Canadians-to those in small communities, to passengers and to others. There are railway employees who are having heart attacks at 49 and 50 years of age. Some of them die, some are demoted. At this time there are 50 railway employees paying $500 contempt of court charges because of such concerns.
One hour on the road, then stop for breakfast.

I am not suggesting anything like that. I am suggesting that there should be regulations covering someone who has completed eight hours of work, so that he can be a judge of his condition in deciding whether or not to carry on. This is my question. It has nothing to do with contracts or interference. It is the responsibility of the minister.
I will conclude with the following note. If the minister does not carry out his responsibility, it will be on his conscience. On top of this, he is allowing American trains to come into Canada. Those employees do not have union contracts or working agreements. They are coming into our country with no agreements, and they must work long hours. They are travelling through the same communities. It is a serious problem. The Minister of Transport has a responsibility to ensure the safety of our communities, of passengers on trains and of the public.

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for

In 1972, the then minister of labour appointed a commission of inquiry, pursuant to Section 62 of the Canada Labour Code, into employment practices related to a variety of classes of railway employees within the legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada which are known collectively as the operating trades or running trades. When the commission reported to the minister on October 16, 1972, it recommended that these employees be exempted from the application of Sections 29 and 30 of the Canada Labour Code because the sections could not be reasonably applied to this class of employee. In consequence thereof, and following further study by the minister, regulation No. SOR-73-246 dated May 9, 1973 was promulgated in the Canada Gazette. In essence, the regulation exempted the cited classes of employees from the application of Sections 29 and 30 of Part III of the Canada Labour Code. For the purposes of these regulations, hours of work are scheduled and actually worked without regard to Section 31. of the code.
It should be noted that the classes of employees who are exempt from the application of the hours of work under the provision in Part III of the Canada Labour Code are generally engaged in work in which it would be impossible to demand crew changes at the end of any given eight-hour work period.
